forces.title: Strait of Hormuz disruption poses significant global energy supply shock
forces.description: The ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruption, categorized as the largest recent energy supply shock, has affected approximately 20 percent of global oil and LNG supply. Its on-and-off closure, combined with other regional disruptions, creates substantial uncertainty for global energy markets, directly impacting integrated oil and gas companies' upstream, midstream (LNG transport), and downstream (crude supply for refining) operations due to supply chain risks and price volatility.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Depleting strategic crude and refined product inventories globally
forces.description: Strategic petroleum reserves (SPR) and other inventories, which cushioned the initial shock from the Strait of Hormuz, are thinning rapidly. The US SPR declined to less than 300 million barrels by late August 2026, near historical minimums. Refined product inventories are even thinner and fragmented by fuel and location. This depletion reduces critical buffers for integrated oil and gas companies, increasing their exposure to future supply disruptions and price volatility across their value chains.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Global refining system under significant pressure, leading to product shortages
forces.description: The global refining system is facing severe pressure, with Gulf refineries cutting output and significant Russian refining capacity offline. Other regions' refineries are running at near full capacity but suffer efficiency losses due to adapting to suboptimal crude grades, leading to lower yields of high-demand products like jet fuel and diesel. This strain creates bottlenecks for integrated oil and gas companies' downstream operations, impacting refined product supply, margins, and potentially leading to localized scarcity.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Significant rewiring of global oil and refined products trade flows
forces.description: More than one out of every five barrels of seaborne oil traded in Q2 2026 was rewired compared to pre-crisis flows, driven by inventory releases, bypass pipelines, and new production. China curtailed imports, while the United States increased exports, helping Europe and South Korea. This fundamental shift in trade routes and partnerships impacts the logistics, procurement strategies, and market access for integrated oil and gas companies, necessitating adaptation to new supply corridors and market dynamics.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Benchmark gas prices in Europe and Asia nearly doubled due to LNG disruption
forces.description: Physical damage to liquefaction units in the Gulf, representing 17 percent of Qatar’s export capacity or 3 percent of global LNG supply, is expected to take three to five years to rebuild. This, combined with slower inventory buildup in Europe, led benchmark gas prices in Europe and Asia to nearly double their previous-year value by late August 2026, creating significant cost pressures and supply uncertainty for integrated oil and gas companies with LNG operations or gas-fired assets.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: LNG buyers prioritizing geographic diversification and flexibility in procurement
forces.description: Following the Strait of Hormuz disruption, 93% of LNG buyers globally plan to increase suppliers and geographic diversification in the next two to three years, including 80% of European buyers. Additionally, 60% are seeking greater flexibility and portfolio optimization, and 52% are strengthening contractual protections, particularly force majeure clauses. This structural shift requires integrated oil and gas companies to adapt their LNG supply portfolios, invest in new infrastructure, and renegotiate contracts to meet evolving buyer demands for security and resilience.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: Increased investment in LNG supply resilience measures by companies
forces.description: Approximately 66 percent of LNG buyers globally, including those in Europe, are planning to increase investment in resilience measures such as storage infrastructure (30%), shipping (19%), upstream equity (17%), floating storage and regasification units (FSRUs) (15%), and regasification capacity (13%). This focus on bolstering LNG infrastructure and supply chain control presents significant investment opportunities and strategic advantages for integrated oil and gas companies with a strong presence in the LNG value chain.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: Norway discussing new oil and gas capacity amidst energy security drive
forces.description: Amidst global energy security concerns, Norway is actively discussing plans for new oil and gas capacity. This initiative, also seen in the United Kingdom, aims to diversify production and reduce exposure to geopolitical chokepoints. For integrated oil and gas companies operating in Norway, this signals a potential tailwind for upstream exploration and production activities, offering opportunities for new projects and increased output within Europe's energy supply landscape.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Accelerated electrification in the European Union impacting fuel demand
forces.description: Electrification, driven by technologies like electric vehicles (EVs) and heat pumps, is accelerating in the European Union, with EV sales growing over 30 percent in Q2 2026. New policy measures like AccelerateEU support further electrification. While this offers environmental benefits, it represents a structural shift away from traditional fossil fuels in end uses. Integrated oil and gas companies with significant downstream operations face a long-term headwind on demand for refined products like gasoline and diesel, necessitating diversification and investment in alternative energy solutions.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Persistent and under-estimated growth in global energy demand
forces.description: Global energy demand continues to rise, increasing by 1.3 percent in 2025, driven by factors such as higher cooling demand across Asia, expanding freight and petrochemical sectors, significant data center growth, and industrial capacity expansion through reshoring. This sustained demand, often underestimated by previous outlooks, creates a persistent tailwind for integrated oil and gas companies, supporting demand for both traditional fossil fuels and the infrastructure to deliver them, even as the energy transition progresses.
forces.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

forces.title: Underfunded critical energy infrastructure (grids, transmission, storage)
forces.description: While generation capacity is expanding, the necessary infrastructure to connect, balance, and secure energy supply, including grids, transmission, storage, and dispatchable backup, remains underfunded and underbuilt. Transmission build-out in major markets lags far behind generation due to long connection queues and complex permitting. This poses a significant risk to the overall energy system's reliability and resilience, potentially creating bottlenecks that hinder the effective integration of new energy sources and could necessitate reliance on existing, more stable energy carriers from integrated oil and gas companies in the medium term.
forces.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

forces.title: AI adoption in upstream operations driving efficiency and value creation
forces.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is providing a significant step change in value for upstream oil and gas companies, with top use cases driving nearly half of the identified $65 billion near-term value. AI advancements are improving productivity, enhancing safety, and boosting exploration success, with potential for autonomous operating modes. This presents a substantial upside driver for integrated oil and gas companies to optimize their upstream assets, reduce costs, and improve returns through strategic investment in AI capabilities.
forces.source_title: Can upstream oil and gas produce value from AI’s $230 billion pay zone?

forces.title: Record high jet fuel prices due to Middle East conflict
forces.description: The Middle East conflict has driven jet fuel prices to record highs in early 2026, increasing costs by 130%. This directly impacts airfreight expenses and poses a risk of commercial flight cancellations, which further amplifies freight costs. For integrated oil and gas companies, this represents a significant headwind for their downstream marketing and retail segments, particularly concerning aviation turbine fuel (ATF) sales and profitability, while also contributing to broader economic inflation and supply chain issues.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: Global energy system proving resilient to shocks, but limits are becoming apparent
viewpoints.description: The global energy system has shown greater resilience than expected during the Strait of Hormuz crisis, due to temporary buffers like bypass pipelines and inventories. However, these measures have limits, with inventories thinning and the refining system under stress. This suggests that while immediate shocks can be absorbed, the system's long-term vulnerabilities persist, requiring structural changes to enhance energy security for integrated oil and gas companies.
viewpoints.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: Energy security concerns are fundamentally reshaping the business case for resilience investments
viewpoints.description: Growing energy security concerns are redefining the strategic imperative for resilience. While such measures require upfront investment, they offer significant long-term benefits including cost reduction, business continuity, and potential for growth amidst volatility. Decision-makers in integrated oil and gas need to map their exposure across fuels, assets, and routes, and act on improving efficiency, flexibility in inputs, suppliers, and logistics to secure future operations.
viewpoints.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: Most LNG buyers expect structural shifts in procurement strategies due to disruption
viewpoints.description: Approximately 80 percent of LNG buyers anticipate changes in their procurement strategies due to the Strait of Hormuz disruption, with nearly half expecting structural shifts. This sentiment is particularly strong among Asian buyers, though 80% of European buyers also expect changes. This implies a significant move away from cost minimization towards prioritizing security of supply, driving integrated oil and gas companies with LNG portfolios to reassess their supply chain resilience.
viewpoints.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

viewpoints.title: Fossil fuels and renewables are growing in parallel, with peak oil demand still elusive
viewpoints.description: Contrary to assumptions, 2025 data shows both fossil fuels and renewables are growing, with fossil fuels adding more energy in absolute terms. Global oil demand increased by 1.3 MMb/d and coal consumption hit record levels. This indicates that the long-predicted peak for fossil fuels remains elusive, and integrated oil and gas companies face a complex landscape where both traditional and low-carbon energy sources are expanding to meet increasing global demand.
viewpoints.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

viewpoints.title: Middle East conflict triggers high energy inflation and widespread supply chain disruption
viewpoints.description: The ongoing Middle East conflict is causing significant energy inflation and widespread supply chain disruption, particularly if the Strait of Hormuz remains impacted. This affects global oil and gas supply, leading to price spikes and increased freight costs. For integrated oil and gas companies, this translates into higher input costs, potential supply risks, and elevated operational expenses, especially for their downstream and marketing segments, impacting profitability and supply security.
viewpoints.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Developments & Insights May 2026

viewpoints.title: AI can unlock significant value for upstream oil and gas companies
viewpoints.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to deliver substantial value in the upstream oil and gas sector, with an estimated $65 billion in annual recurring value in the near term and a credible path to $230 billion at full potential. AI-driven improvements in exploration success could also unlock over $35 billion annually in balance sheet value. This presents a significant opportunity for integrated oil and gas companies to enhance efficiency, safety, and exploration outcomes across their upstream operations.
viewpoints.source_title: Can upstream oil and gas produce value from AI’s $230 billion pay zone?

demand_drivers.description: Driven by cooling demand in Asia, expansion in freight and petrochemicals, significant data center growth, and accelerating industrial capacity from reshoring efforts, pushing for parallel growth in all energy carriers.

market_sizing.methodology: Total global investment in all aspects of the energy system. Of this, $1.8 trillion was directed towards fossil fuels, power generation, and low-carbon technologies.
market_sizing.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

demand_drivers.description: AI enhances productivity through faster seismic processing, optimized maintenance, and reduced nonproductive drilling time.
AI-driven improvements could unlock over $35 billion annually in balance sheet value through reserves accretion.
Maturity of AI technology enabling autonomous drilling sequences and generative work-pack creation.

pnl_drivers.description: AI reduces operational costs and improves output, but poses challenges to traditional commercial models where efficiency reduces activity rewarded by contracts.

new_opportunities.description: Building AI-native workflows that transform data libraries into platforms can create significant value, especially for players able to industrialize AI across the organization.

market_sizing.methodology: Bottom-up sizing of over 550 AI use cases across the upstream value chain stages for oil and gas and oilfield services and equipment (OFSE) companies, representing full potential. Near-term value with today's technology estimated at $65 billion annually. Net of implementation costs over $30 billion.
market_sizing.source_title: Can upstream oil and gas produce value from AI’s $230 billion pay zone?
